title: Open Question: Minimum Collision Number in Cube Dissections
content: The header states the open question and context. Every cube dissection must have at least one collision pair (Wiedijk #82), but how many cubes must be 'colliding' (sharing size with some other cube)? This file proves the lower bound is 2, and formally states the open question: is 2 achievable? The file imports DissectionOfCubes for the main impossibility theorem, and opens the DissectionOfCubes namespace.
mathContext: A *collision pair* is $(c_1, c_2)$ with $c_1, c_2 \in d$, $c_1 \neq c_2$, and $c_1.\text{size} = c_2.\text{size}$. The *colliding cubes* set is $\{c \in d \mid \exists c' \in d,\, c \neq c' \wedge c.\text{size} = c'.\text{size}\}$.

title: Every Nonempty Dissection Has a Collision Pair
content: The theorem every_dissection_has_collision derives a collision pair from the main impossibility theorem. The proof unfolds allDifferentSizes (the hypothesis of dissection_of_cubes), applies push_neg to convert ¬∀ into ∃, and extracts the collision pair. IsCollisionPair is defined as a conjunction: both cubes are in the dissection, they are distinct, and they have the same size.
mathContext:
From $
eg orall c_1 \in d,\,  orall c_2 \in d,\, c_1 
eq c_2 \Rightarrow c_1.	ext{size} 
eq c_2.	ext{size}$, push_neg gives $\exists c_1 \in d,\, \exists c_2 \in d,\, c_1 
eq c_2 \wedge c_1.	ext{size} = c_2.	ext{size}$.

title: Size Classes: Cubes Sharing a Given Size
content: The sizeClass is a noncomputable Finset containing all cubes in the dissection with the same side length as a given cube c. It uses Classical.decEq for Cube since equality of real-valued structures is not constructively decidable. Two theorems follow: mem_sizeClass_self (every cube is in its own size class) and collision_class_at_least_two (if c has a collision partner, its size class has ≥ 2 members, proved via Finset.one_lt_card by exhibiting c and its partner as distinct members).
mathContext: \[\text{sizeClass}(d, c) = \{c' \in d.\text{cubes} \mid c'.\text{size} = c.\text{size}\}\] Using classical decidability: `haveI : DecidableEq Cube := Classical.decEq _`.

title: At Least 2 Colliding Cubes: The Key Lower Bound
content: The collidingCubes Finset contains all cubes participating in any collision. The main theorem at_least_two_colliding_cubes shows its cardinality is ≥ 2 for any nonempty dissection. Proof: extract a collision pair (c₁, c₂) from every_dissection_has_collision; show both c₁ and c₂ are in collidingCubes (c₁ witnesses c₂ as its partner, c₂ witnesses c₁ with Ne.symm); then {c₁, c₂} ⊆ collidingCubes, so 2 = card{c₁,c₂} ≤ card(collidingCubes).
mathContext: \[\text{collidingCubes}(d) = \{c \in d \mid \exists c' \in d,\, c \neq c' \wedge c.\text{size} = c'.\text{size}\}\] Key step: $|\{c_1, c_2\}| = 2 \leq |\text{collidingCubes}(d)|$ via `Finset.card_pair` and `Finset.card_le_card`.

title: HasMinimalCollision: The Formal Open Question
content: HasMinimalCollision d is defined as (collidingCubes d).card = 2 — the lower bound of 2 is achieved. The OPEN QUESTION is whether any valid dissection satisfies this. The difficulty is that covers_unit_cube is a placeholder (True) in our formalization, so proving geometric achievability requires the actual tiling constraint. The volume argument gives informal evidence: 2 cubes of size s contribute 2s³ to the total volume, but actual geometric tiling further constrains the configuration.
mathContext: \[\exists d : \text{CubeDissection},\, d.\text{cubes}.\text{Nonempty} \wedge |\text{collidingCubes}(d)| = 2\] This is the open question. For a HasMinimalCollision dissection, if the two colliding cubes have size $s$, the remaining cubes have distinct sizes $s_1, \ldots, s_{n-2}$ with $2s^3 + s_1^3 + \cdots + s_{n-2}^3 = 1$.

title: Floor Argument: Why Cascades Force Many Collisions
content: This section explains geometrically why the minimum number might be much larger than 2. Littlewood's infinite descent creates a cascade: smallest cube on floor → smaller cubes above it → even smaller cubes above those → .... At each level, many cubes must collectively tile the cross-section. The geometric constraints at each level typically require multiple cubes of similar (but different by assumption) sizes, which eventually forces many size repetitions. Whether this cascade can be arranged to produce only one repeated size is the geometric heart of the open question.
mathContext: The floor argument: at height $h$, the cross-section $[0,1]^2 \times \{h\}$ is covered by cubes. If the smallest cube $C$ at height $h$ has side $s$, then above $C$ is a new floor at height $h + s$, covered by cubes smaller than $s$. The cascade: $s_0 > s_1 > s_2 > \cdots$ eventually terminates (finitely many cubes), forcing repetitions.

title: 2D Contrast: Squared Squares vs Cubed Cubes
content: The 2D analog of the problem has a completely different answer. A square CAN be dissected into squares of all different sizes ('perfect squared square'). The first example was found in 1940 by Brooks, Smith, Stone, and Tutte. The smallest simple perfect squared square (no perfect squared rectangle sub-tiling) has 21 squares. In 2D, the minimum number of 'colliding' squares in any dissection of a rectangle (which cannot be perfectly squared) is studied but not fully resolved. The 3D case is harder because interior cubes are completely surrounded, unlike 2D edge effects.
mathContext: In 2D: $\exists$ perfect tiling of a square with all-different sizes (squared squares). In 3D: $\nexists$ perfect tiling (Wiedijk #82). The analog: min$|$collidingCubes$|$ over all valid 3D dissections is unknown; min$|$collidingSquares$|$ over all valid 2D dissections of rectangles is also not fully determined.
